name: Hamun Lakes
description: The Hamun Lakes form a shallow, seasonally changing wetland complex across the Iran–Afghanistan border in the Sistan Basin. River inflows sustain freshwater habitats and livelihoods, while prolonged drought and upstream water withdrawals increase exposure of the lakebed and the risk of dust storms. [s1][s3]

seo.title: Hamun Lakes: Sistan’s Changing Border Wetlands | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore the Hamun wetland complex, its dependence on river inflows, its seasonal ecology, and the connections between drying lakes and dust.

content.heading: A wetland complex with shifting boundaries
content.content:
The Hamun Lakes, also spelled Hamoun, are best understood as a connected wetland landscape rather than a single lake with a permanent shoreline. Hamun-e-Puzak, Hamun-e-Saberi and Hamun-e-Helmand occupy the Sistan Basin along the Iran–Afghanistan border. The Ramsar wetland information sheet describes a system receiving water from the Helmand, also called Hirmand, the Farah River and smaller rivers originating in Afghanistan. Ramsar is the international convention concerned with wetland conservation. [s1]

These waters collect in an internally drained basin: they do not follow an ordinary river outlet to the ocean. Nevertheless, the lakes can be predominantly fresh rather than uniformly saline. The historical Ramsar account explains that large floods can pass through the connected lakes and flush salts toward a terminal depression farther southeast. Connections between individual lakes therefore matter alongside the total amount of incoming water. [s1]

content.heading: Seasonal drying and prolonged loss are different
content.content:
Water levels normally rise in spring and decline through the following months. Large areas can dry during this regular cycle. The US Geological Survey explains that the wetlands’ shallowness makes their extent particularly sensitive to changing inflows; irrigation expansion increases their vulnerability when drought arrives. During prolonged dry periods, fishing becomes impossible and birds move elsewhere. [s2]

A dry-season photograph consequently cannot, by itself, establish that the whole complex has permanently disappeared. The USGS image sequence spans several decades, but its scenes were captured in different months. They document changing conditions without constituting a directly comparable annual measurement series. Reading those images requires attention to both the observation date and the seasonal water cycle. [s2]

content.heading: An inhabited landscape under pressure
content.content:
NASA’s historical account describes fishing, livestock keeping, farming and reed-boat use around the wetlands. Water supported an inhabited landscape whose livelihoods depended on the relationship between rivers, marsh vegetation and shallow lakes. Its reconstruction of late twentieth-century change identified irrigation development, dams, urban expansion and severe drought as interacting pressures. That account concerns a historical episode; its descriptions of devastation should not be presented as a survey of conditions today. [s4]

The distinction between water returning and a lasting recovery is therefore essential. Renewed flooding can change the visible landscape, while the reliability of future river deliveries remains a separate question. NASA’s account emphasizes multiple causes and uncertainty about their relative contributions, rather than assigning the entire decline to one intervention. [s4]

content.heading: When exposed lakebed becomes a dust source
content.content:
The consequences extend beyond the shoreline. NASA’s February 2023 assessment links persistent drought and upstream withdrawals to shrinking wetlands, reduced vegetation and exposed sediment. Strong winds can lift that material into the atmosphere. Dust events are most frequent in summer but can occur in other seasons when the lakebed is dry. [s3]

Satellite observations documented dust streaming from the exposed bed in January 2023, with modeled transport extending beyond the immediate basin. This establishes a connection between wetland condition and a wider atmospheric hazard. It does not establish a precise water level or inundated area at the editorial cutoff. The most useful way to understand Hamun is as a variable river-fed system whose ecological and social functions depend on recurring water delivery. [s3]

content.title: How wetland drying can increase dust exposure
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Persistent drought"] -->|"Can reduce water availability"| C["Reduced wetland inundation"]
  B["Upstream water withdrawals"] -->|"Can reduce river deliveries"| C
  C -->|"Reduces cover"| D["Less wetland vegetation"]
  C -->|"Exposes"| E["Dry lakebed sediment"]
  D -->|"Leaves sediment less protected"| E
  E -->|"Strong winds can entrain particles"| F["Airborne dust"]
```
content.summary: The arrows describe mechanisms documented by NASA. They do not quantify the separate contributions of drought and withdrawals or imply that every dry episode produces the same dust conditions.

name: Namak Lake
description: Namak Lake is a largely dry saline lake at the terminus of an internally drained basin in north-central Iran. Its setting connects mountain-fed rivers and heavily used upstream catchments with an evaporative lowland landscape south of Tehran. [s1]

seo.title: Namak Lake: Salt, Seasonal Water and a Closed Basin | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Namak Lake’s saline landscape, its mountain-to-basin water connections, and why published lake-area figures require careful interpretation.

content.heading: A lake defined by its basin
content.content:
Namak Lake, recorded as Daryacheh-ye Namak in the International Association for Great Lakes Research inventory, is a salt lake in Iran’s arid interior. Its name should be tied to this specific location: a generic reference to a salt lake is not enough to identify the feature. The association’s profile places it in a cold-desert climate and classifies its water as saline. [s2]

The Freshwater Ecoregions of the World account describes the surrounding drainage basin as endorheic, meaning that its waters terminate inland. It distinguishes Namak from Howz-e Soltan, another salt lake in the same depression. These are related geographic features, not interchangeable names for a single water surface. Understanding that distinction helps prevent photographs, measurements and environmental claims from being assigned to the wrong lake. [s1]

content.heading: From mountain catchments to an evaporative lowland
content.content:
The basin is framed by the Alborz Mountains to the north and the Zagros to the west. Its river network includes the Karaj and Jajrud catchments and the Qom and Qareh Su rivers. Snowmelt from surrounding mountains helps supply the drainage system, while the lowland terminus is largely dry. The ecoregion account describes spring inundation followed by evaporation into summer. This is a seasonal description, not a guarantee of water in a particular year. [s1]

The contrast between uplands and lowlands is also important in hydrological research. A peer-reviewed study of the Namak basin describes predominantly arid lowlands alongside wetter highland environments. Basin-wide averages can therefore conceal differences between where precipitation falls, where runoff forms and where water ultimately collects. The lake is the downstream expression of a much larger landscape. [s3]

content.heading: Why a single area figure can mislead
content.content:
Published inventories do not provide one consistent surface-area figure for Namak. The IAGLR profile and the ecoregion account report different values without a common observation date or a shared measurement protocol. They should not be interpreted as successive measurements demonstrating expansion or contraction. A defensible comparison would first need to establish whether each figure represents open water, the lakebed or another mapped boundary. [s1][s2]

For this reason, this page does not present a fixed current area or turn those inventory entries into a trend. The same caution applies to depth: a catalogue entry does not describe the spatial distribution of water across a shallow seasonal basin, and it cannot establish conditions at the research cutoff. [s2]

content.heading: Reading evidence of water stress
content.content:
Research on low streamflows provides a more specific view of changing water conditions upstream. A study covering 1970–2015 examined seasonal low flows at hydrometric stations across the Namak basin and found widespread declines. It investigated associations with rainfall and temperature, including differences between seasons. Those findings concern river-flow behavior over the study period; they are not measurements of the lake’s annual area. [s3]

The distinction matters when interpreting environmental change. Evidence that low flows declined can support concern about the basin’s hydrology, while assigning a precise share of lake drying to climate, withdrawals or individual dams requires additional analysis. Namak is most clearly understood through these connected scales: the saline terminal lake, the river network feeding its basin and the climatic conditions influencing that network. [s3]

name: Rivers & Water Resources
description: Iran’s water geography combines mountain-fed rivers, internally drained basins and groundwater systems that sustain settlements and agriculture. Understanding water availability requires distinguishing seasonal flows, stored water, extraction and replenishment rather than treating them as interchangeable measures. [s1][s2][s4]

seo.title: Iran’s Rivers, Groundwater and Water Resources | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran’s contrasting drainage regions, groundwater systems, qanats and water infrastructure, with guidance on interpreting water-resource evidence.

content.heading: Where water goes
content.content:
Iran’s rivers make more sense when read through drainage basins: areas whose runoff converges toward a common destination. Much of the country drains internally, while western mountain catchments carry water toward the Persian Gulf. In the north, streams descend toward the Caspian Sea. Although these rivers leave their local mountain basins, the Caspian itself has no outlet to the world ocean. [s1]

This geography creates pronounced regional contrasts. The northern slopes of the Alborz receive more moisture than the plateau to their south. In the west, Zagros catchments gather water into extensive river systems. Interior and eastern regions generally have much more limited surface runoff. A map showing river channels alone therefore gives an incomplete impression of dependable water availability. [s1]

Seasonality matters as much as direction. Rain, snow storage and subsequent melt influence when rivers carry water. A river’s spring flow and its late-summer minimum describe different conditions; neither should be substituted for its annual discharge. These distinctions are fundamental to comparing rivers, reservoirs and the demands placed on them. [s1]

content.heading: The water beneath the river map
content.content:
Groundwater is water stored below the surface in geological formations called aquifers. Research on Iran distinguishes fractured and dissolved limestone systems in the west, alluvial aquifers in sediment-filled plains, and coastal aquifers beside marine and inland waters. Western karst aquifers help recharge rivers including the Dez, Karun and Karkheh. Surface water and groundwater are thus connected parts of a hydrological system. [s2]

A national study using water-management records from 2002–2015 documented groundwater depletion and salinization. Its historical coverage is important: it provides evidence of sustained pressure during that interval, not a direct reading of aquifer conditions in 2026. The authors also explained that later data with comparable spatial and temporal resolution were unavailable to their analysis. [s2]

The study found that declining extraction could accompany worsening resource conditions. Less water pumped does not necessarily mean successful conservation if depletion or salinity has reduced usable supplies. Interpreting withdrawal statistics therefore requires evidence about water levels, quality and recharge alongside the amount extracted. The paper discusses both physical constraints and possible management effects rather than treating a falling withdrawal total as self-explanatory. [s2]

content.heading: Qanats: infrastructure and shared allocation
content.content:
A qanat conveys groundwater through a gently sloping underground tunnel, allowing gravity to carry it from an aquifer toward a lower outlet. UNESCO’s account of the Persian Qanat describes systems tapping alluvial aquifers near valley heads and supplying agricultural land and permanent settlements in arid regions. Their significance lies in making groundwater accessible through a built landscape of tunnels and associated facilities. [s3]

UNESCO also emphasizes communal systems for sharing and distributing water. The heritage is consequently institutional as well as technical: maintaining a channel and allocating its discharge are related tasks. This description concerns the selected World Heritage systems and their documented traditions. It should not be read as proof that every surviving qanat has adequate water, remains operational or follows identical allocation arrangements. [s3]

content.heading: Reading water statistics correctly
content.content:
FAO’s AQUASTAT separates water resources, withdrawals, irrigation, wastewater and related indicators. These answer different questions. A resource estimate describes availability under a defined method; a withdrawal figure describes abstraction; an irrigation-area measure describes land equipped or used under its stated definition. They cannot be exchanged simply because all concern water. [s4]

The inspected AQUASTAT database guide also explains a reporting structure that groups observations into multi-year periods and displays the latest available observation within each period. Such entries must retain their actual reference years. They should not be expanded into a complete annual record by repeating values across intervening years. [s4]

For this guide, annual charts require comparable observations with clear dates and definitions. The sources examined establish the importance of groundwater monitoring and basin geography, but they did not yield a validated annual national series for the latest fifteen-year window. Presenting that gap explicitly is more informative than a chart whose apparent continuity exceeds the evidence. [s2][s4]

content.heading: Explore the systems in detail
content.content:
The pages in this branch follow the Karun, Zayandeh Rud, Sefidrud, Aras, Karkheh and Helmand individually, alongside separate guides to dams and reservoirs and to springs and waterfalls. Each offers a different entry point into the same questions: where water originates, where it travels, how its timing changes and which uses depend on it.

Begin with the basin, then examine the evidence at the appropriate scale. A national groundwater study, a river gauge and a reservoir observation each reveal something useful, but none alone describes the whole system.
